topics.title: Sampling distributions & standard error
topics.summary: Separate individual observations from averages. Then identify the center, spread, and shape of the statistic you are using.

sections.title: Population, sample, statistic, parameter
sections.body: A parameter describes a population: μ is its mean, σ its standard deviation, and p its proportion. A statistic describes one sample: x̄, s, and p̂. A sampling distribution asks what a statistic would look like over repeated random samples of the SAME size. It is different from the distribution of the individual observations.
sections.formula: E(x̄) = μ; SD(x̄) = SE(x̄) = σ / √n
sections.example: If individual commute times average 30 minutes with SD 12, sample means from n=36 are centered at 30 with SE=12/6=2 minutes. Individual people still have SD 12.
sections.trap: The sampling distribution is not the list of observations in one sample, and its center does not move toward zero as n increases.
sections.source: Sampling Distribution, slides 2–5, 14; Practice Exam, Q1, Q7

sections.title: Standard deviation versus standard error
sections.body: SD measures the spread of individual values. SE measures the spread of sample statistics. When σ is unknown, use s to estimate the SE of x̄. A small SE means averages vary little across repeated samples; it does not mean individual people or products are similar.
sections.formula:
Known σ: SE = σ / √n
Unknown σ: estimated SE = s / √n
Variance of x̄ = σ² / n
sections.example: With σ=20 and n=64, SE=20/8=2.5. The variance of x̄ is 6.25; it is not the SE.
sections.trap: Divide by √n, not n. Do not confuse a variance, a standard deviation, and a standard error.
sections.source: Sampling Distribution, slides 8–12, 14; CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 2–3

sections.title: What increasing n changes
sections.body: A larger random sample makes the sampling distribution narrower because SE is proportional to 1/√n. The population SD and population mean do not change merely because we sample more people. The sample mean is still random; a larger n does not guarantee an exact estimate.
sections.formula: SE(new) / SE(old) = √(n_old / n_new)
sections.example: To cut SE from 4 to 2, multiply n by 4. Doubling n multiplies SE by 1/√2, about 0.707.
sections.trap: Doubling sample size does not halve SE. More data also does not automatically fix selection bias.
sections.source: Sampling Distribution, slides 9–10, 14; CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 3–4

sections.title: When can you use the normal curve?
sections.body: If the population is normal, its sample mean is normal for any n under independent sampling. Otherwise, the Central Limit Theorem gives an approximately normal sampling distribution for sufficiently large n with finite population variance. This course uses n≈30 as the usual rule of thumb. Severe skew, outliers, or heavy tails can require much more data.
sections.formula:
For a normal/approximately normal x̄:
z = (x̄ − μ) / (σ / √n)
sections.example: A skewed population sampled at n=64 can often be analyzed with a normal approximation for the mean. This does not make the individual observations normally distributed.
sections.trap: The CLT is about the mean’s distribution. It does not say every population becomes normal or that n=30 is a universal guarantee.
sections.source: Sampling Distribution, slides 13–14; CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slide 4; Practice Exam, Q2

sections.title: Sampling probabilities & Excel recognition
sections.body: First decide whether a question concerns one observation X or a sample mean x̄. Use σ for X and σ/√n for x̄. Excel NORM.DIST(x,mean,SD,TRUE) gives a LEFT cumulative area; subtract from 1 for a right-tail probability. TRUE and 1 are equivalent cumulative arguments.
sections.formula:
P(x̄ > a) = 1 − NORM.DIST(a, μ, σ/SQRT(n), TRUE)
P(a < x̄ < b) = F(b) − F(a)
sections.example: For μ=80, σ=10, n=25, P(x̄>84) uses SE=2, z=2, and is about .0228. The Excel expression is =1-NORM.DIST(84,80,10/SQRT(25),TRUE).
sections.trap: A formula may have the correct tail but the wrong spread. Check BOTH the 1− and the division by SQRT(n).
sections.source: Sampling Distribution, slides 10, 14; Practice Exam, Q6

topics.title: Confidence intervals for means
topics.summary: Use estimate ± critical value × standard error. The known-versus-unknown population SD determines z versus t.

sections.title: What a confidence interval actually says
sections.body: The population mean is fixed; intervals change from sample to sample. A 95% method captures the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples when assumptions hold. For one computed interval, say “we are 95% confident that the population mean lies between the endpoints.” This is about a population mean, not the percentage of individual data inside the interval.
sections.formula:
CI = point estimate ± margin of error
Margin of error (ME) = critical value × SE
α = 1 − confidence LEVEL
sections.example: For a CI of (42,58), x̄=50 and ME=8. The interval estimates μ. It does not claim that 95% of people have values from 42 to 58.
sections.trap: On an MCQ, choose the repeated-sampling interpretation rather than “there is a 95% probability the fixed μ is in this computed interval.”
sections.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 5–7; CI Proportions, slides 3–5; Practice Exam, Q8

sections.title: Population σ known: use z
sections.body: When the population standard deviation σ is supplied as known, use the standard normal critical value. Conditions include random, sufficiently independent observations and a normal or sufficiently well-behaved large-sample distribution for x̄.
sections.example: With x̄=52, σ=7, n=49 and 95% confidence: SE=1, ME=1.96, so CI=(50.04,53.96).
sections.trap: A population MEAN being specified does not make σ known. Read whether the given spread is population σ or sample s.
sections.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 6–7; Practice Exam, Q9

sections.title: Population σ unknown: use t
sections.body: Replace unknown σ with sample SD s, and use Student’s t with df=n−1 for one sample. The t curve is symmetric with heavier tails than the standard normal; it approaches normal as df grows. For small samples, a roughly normal population without serious outliers is especially important.
sections.formula:
CI for μ = x̄ ± t* × s/√n
df = n − 1
sections.example: With n=16, x̄=18, s=4, and supplied t*=2.131: SE=1 and CI=(15.869,20.131).
sections.trap: Use df=n−1, not n. A large n does not make a supplied sample s become a known population σ; t remains the standard choice.
sections.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 8–10; Practice Exam, Q12, Q14

sections.title: How the interval gets wider or narrower
sections.body: At a fixed confidence level, larger n narrows the interval and greater variability widens it. At a fixed dataset, higher confidence requires a larger critical value, so the interval widens. Changing confidence changes the margin, not the point estimate. To achieve a desired ME with known σ, solve the ME equation for n and round UP.
sections.formula:
Width = 2 × ME
Known-σ planning: n ≥ (z*σ / desired ME)²
sections.example: Going from 95% to 99% confidence makes a CI wider. At the same confidence level and σ, cutting ME in half requires four times n.
sections.trap: “More confidence” does not mean “more precise.” Wider intervals have higher coverage but lower precision. The planning formula is algebra from the z interval.
sections.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 3, 6–7; Practice Exam, Q11, Q13

sections.title: Excel critical values, and linking CI to a test
sections.body: T.INV.2T(alpha,df) returns the positive two-sided t cutoff: input α, not α/2. T.INV(1−α/2,df) gives the same upper cutoff. NORM.S.INV(1−α/2) gives z*. A two-sided level-α test of a mean using the matching model rejects a candidate μ₀ outside its (1−α) CI.
sections.formula:
90% one-sample t CI with n=20:
=T.INV.2T(0.10,19)
=CONFIDENCE.T(alpha,s,n) returns ME, not endpoints
sections.example: For a 95% CI of (10.2,13.8), μ₀=12 is compatible with the interval; μ₀=14 would be rejected by the matching two-sided 5% test.
sections.trap: Do not feed .05 to T.INV.2T for a 90% CI. Do not mistake CONFIDENCE.T’s margin of error for an upper endpoint.
sections.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slide 10; CI Proportions, slide 12; Practice Exam, Q14

topics.title: Proportions: intervals & pooled tests
topics.summary: Recognize success/failure data. CI standard errors estimate the population proportions; equality tests use the null’s pooled proportion.

sections.title: One proportion: build the interval
sections.body: A proportion is appropriate when outcomes can be classified as success/failure. Estimate the population proportion p using p̂=x/n, where x is the number of successes. For the usual normal-approximation CI, estimate SE using p̂, then add and subtract z* times that SE.
sections.formula:
p̂ = x/n
SE = √[p̂(1−p̂)/n]
CI for p = p̂ ± z*√[p̂(1−p̂)/n]
sections.example: If 240 of 400 customers prefer a product, p̂=.60 and SE≈.0245. A 95% CI is .60±1.96(.0245)≈(.552,.648).
sections.trap: Enter percentages as proportions: 60% becomes .60. An interval for p estimates a population proportion, not a sample count.
sections.source: CI Proportions, slides 6–10; Practice Exam, Q10

sections.title: Conditions and interpretation
sections.body: Use random, independent observations and enough successes and failures for a normal approximation. The course’s handwritten two-proportion notes require at least 5 of each outcome in each group; some texts use the more conservative cutoff 10. For this course follow the stated convention. Very sparse data need a different method rather than blindly applying a z formula. For a null-based proportion z test, assess expected successes and failures under p₀ (one sample) or the pooled estimate under equality (two samples) as appropriate.
sections.formula:
Successes = n × p̂; failures = n × (1−p̂)
Independent groups: check each group separately
sections.example: With n=100 and p̂=.98 there are only 2 failures. The usual course normal-approximation condition fails even though n is 100.
sections.trap: A large total n is not enough when one outcome is rare. “95% confident” concerns population p, not 95% of responses being successes.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 23, 27–28; CI Proportions, slides 3, 9–10

sections.title: Difference of two proportions: CI uses two estimates
sections.body: For two independent random groups, estimate p₁−p₂ by p̂₁−p̂₂. A CI does not impose equality, so its SE keeps the two separate sample proportions. The order of subtraction must match the question. A positive interval means group 1 has the higher population proportion.
sections.formula: CI for p₁−p₂ = (p̂₁−p̂₂) ± z*√[p̂₁(1−p̂₁)/n₁ + p̂₂(1−p̂₂)/n₂]
sections.example: Group 1: 60/100=.60. Group 2: 90/200=.45. Difference=.15, SE≈.0603; 95% CI≈(.0318,.2682), or 3.18 to 26.82 percentage points.
sections.trap: A .15 proportion difference is 15 percentage points. Do not call it a 15% relative increase unless you calculate the relative change.
sections.source: CI Proportions, slide 11; Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 27–28

sections.title: Test equal proportions: pool under H₀
sections.body: For H₀:p₁=p₂, both samples estimate the same population proportion. Combine successes and observations to estimate that shared p. Then standardize the observed difference using this pooled SE. Choose left, right, or two tails from Hₐ.
sections.formula:
p̂_pool = (x₁+x₂)/(n₁+n₂)
SE₀ = √[p̂_pool(1−p̂_pool)(1/n₁+1/n₂)]
z = (p̂₁−p̂₂) / SE₀  [null difference 0]
sections.example: For 60/100 versus 90/200, p̂_pool=150/300=.50. SE₀≈.06124 and z≈2.449. The .50 is weighted by sample sizes; (.60+.45)/2=.525 would be wrong.
sections.trap: POOL for the usual equality test; do NOT pool for the ordinary difference CI. A pooled test and an unpooled CI need not give exactly identical borderline decisions.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 22–25, 27–28

sections.title: One-proportion test and interval comparisons
sections.body: For a one-proportion z test, the null specifies p₀, so its SE uses p₀ rather than p̂. For CI decisions, a difference interval excluding 0 supports a difference at the matching confidence level. Nonoverlap of two separate CIs supports a difference, but overlap alone does not establish equality; analyze the difference directly.
sections.formula:
One-proportion z = (p̂−p₀) / √[p₀(1−p₀)/n]
Two-sided p-value = 2[1−Φ(|z|)]
sections.example: With p̂=.62, p₀=.50, n=100: SE₀=.05 and z=2.40. A two-sided p-value is about .0164. A CI would instead use √(.62×.38/100).
sections.trap: Do not swap CI SE and null-test SE. A result that fails to reject equality does not prove two populations are identical.
sections.source: Practice Exam, Q22; CI Proportions, slides 12–13; Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 24–28

topics.title: Hypothesis testing: setup, tails & errors
topics.summary: Translate the claim into Hₐ, standardize against H₀, choose the correct tail, and compare p with α.

sections.title: Write the hypotheses before calculating
sections.body: Hypotheses concern a population parameter, such as μ or p, not the observed x̄. The alternative gives the direction: “greater” means >, “less” means <, and “different” means ≠. Equality belongs in H₀. One-sided H₀ may be written as ≤ or ≥; calculations use its boundary value.
sections.formula:
Right: H₀:μ≤μ₀; Hₐ:μ>μ₀
Left: H₀:μ≥μ₀; Hₐ:μ<μ₀
Two-sided: H₀:μ=μ₀; Hₐ:μ≠μ₀
sections.example: A battery maker claims “at least 50 hours.” To challenge that claim, Hₐ:μ<50 and H₀:μ≥50. This is a left-tailed test.
sections.trap: Do not pick the tail after seeing the statistic. The sign of the statistic can disagree with the prespecified direction of Hₐ.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 6–12, 25, 36, 45; Practice Exam, Q19

sections.title: Compute the appropriate test statistic
sections.body: A test statistic asks how many null standard errors the estimate is away from the hypothesized value. Use z for a mean when population σ is known. Use t with df=n−1 when σ is unknown and sample s estimates it. The null value belongs in the numerator.
sections.formula:
Known σ: z = (x̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n)
Unknown σ: t = (x̄−μ₀)/(s/√n); df=n−1
sections.example: With x̄=52, μ₀=50, σ=8, n=64: SE=1 and z=2. With x̄=18.5, μ₀=18, s=2, n=16: SE=.5 and t=1.
sections.trap: Do not subtract sample SD from the sample mean. Do not divide by a variance. A claim about μ₀ being known is separate from σ being known.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 14–15, 27–29, 34–40; Practice Exam, Q20–21

sections.title: P-values, tails, and Excel
sections.body: A p-value is the probability, assuming H₀, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed in the direction(s) of Hₐ. Cumulative distribution functions return left-tail areas. Use 1−CDF for a right tail. For a symmetric two-sided z or t test, double the tail beyond the absolute statistic.
sections.formula:
Left z: =NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE)
Right z: =1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE)
Two-sided z: =2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(z),TRUE))
Left t: =T.DIST(t,df,TRUE)
Right t: =1-T.DIST(t,df,TRUE)
Two-sided t: =T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df)
sections.example: At z=2, right-tail p≈.0228; two-sided p≈.0455. At z=−1.75, two-sided p is 2[1−Φ(1.75)]≈.0801.
sections.trap: For two tails, use |z| or |t| before taking the upper tail. Doubling the upper-tail area at a negative statistic can produce an impossible p>1.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 16–17, 30–31, 41–42; Practice Exam, Q17, Q22

sections.title: Make the decision, then state what it means
sections.body: Reject H₀ when p≤α; otherwise fail to reject H₀. Small p means the observed evidence is unusual under H₀, not that H₀ has that probability of being true. A conclusion should name the population and the alternative direction. Statistical significance does not guarantee a large or practically useful effect.
sections.formula:
p ≤ α → reject H₀
p > α → fail to reject H₀
Right-tail critical rule: statistic > positive cutoff
Two-sided: |statistic| > positive cutoff
sections.example: If p=.032 and α=.05, reject. If α=.01, fail to reject. In the rail example, p=.0285>.01, so fail to reject at 1%.
sections.trap: “Fail to reject” is not “accept H₀” or “prove no effect.” Slide 32’s printed p>.05 is a typo: that example uses α=.01.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 18–19, 32–33, 43–44; Practice Exam, Q18

sections.title: Type I error, Type II error, and power
sections.body: Type I is a false alarm: reject a true H₀. Type II is a missed effect: fail to reject a false H₀. At a fixed sample size, lowering α generally makes rejection harder and increases β. With α fixed, a larger sample generally increases power; the nominal Type I rate remains α.
sections.formula:
P(Type I error | H₀ true) = α
P(Type II error | a specified alternative true) = β
Power = 1−β
sections.example: If H₀ says a product is not defective, a Type I error declares a good product defective. A Type II error misses a truly defective product.
sections.trap: α is not the probability your particular conclusion is wrong. Slide 22’s claim that larger n reduces both errors needs qualification: with fixed α, the Type I rate stays fixed.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 20–22

sections.title: A repeatable MCQ routine
sections.body: Before looking for a formula, identify the variable type and the number of samples. Then identify the parameter, null value, tail, and known versus unknown σ. Compute SE on a separate line; calculate the statistic; compare with p or a critical value; interpret. Excel questions test recognition of the same steps.
sections.formula: Five steps: hypotheses → statistic → decision rule → decision → contextual conclusion
sections.example: “25 independent orders, numeric values, σ unknown, Hₐ:μ>80” means one-sample t, df=24, and right-tail p=1−T.DIST(t,24,TRUE).
sections.trap: Most plausible distractors change exactly one ingredient: tail, df, SE, distribution, or null/estimate. Check these five ingredients deliberately.
sections.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 12–19, 36–44; Practice Exam, Q14, Q17, Q22, Q24

topics.title: Comparing two means
topics.summary: For independent numeric samples, select known-variance z, equal-variance pooled t, or unequal-variance Welch t.

sections.title: Choose the design and the method
sections.body: Two means compare a numeric outcome between two populations. The deck focuses on independent random samples. If population variances are known, use z. If unknown but explicitly assumed equal, use pooled t. If unknown and unequal/not assumed equal, use Welch t. Normality or adequate large-sample behavior is needed, especially with small samples.
sections.formula:
Estimate = x̄₁−x̄₂
Null value = D₀, usually 0
Statistic = [(x̄₁−x̄₂)−D₀] / appropriate SE
sections.example: Comparing purchases from independently sampled Saturday and Sunday shoppers is a two-independent-means setting. Before/after measurements on the same shoppers would be paired; those are not independent groups.
sections.trap: Equal SAMPLE SIZES do not establish equal population variances. A mean problem has numeric outcomes, not counts of success/failure.
sections.source: Two Sample Means, slides 3–6, 8–9, 21–22; paired-design note is a recognition extension

sections.title: Known population variances: two-sample z
sections.body: For independent sample means, variances of their sampling errors add. Use each population variance divided by its sample size. Square root the sum to obtain SE. This is a z method only when the population SDs/variances are known.
sections.formula:
SE = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂)
z = [(x̄₁−x̄₂)−D₀] / SE
sections.example: With σ₁=6, n₁=36, σ₂=8, n₂=64, SE=√(1+1)=√2. A difference of 3 against D₀=0 gives z≈2.121.
sections.trap: Add variances before taking the square root. Do not simply add σ₁/√n₁ and σ₂/√n₂.
sections.source: Two Sample Means, slide 5

sections.title: Unknown but equal variances: pool first
sections.body: The pooled variance is a degrees-of-freedom-weighted average of the two sample variances. Larger samples receive more weight. After finding sₚ², use the same pooled variance for both terms of the SE, then a t distribution with n₁+n₂−2 degrees of freedom.
sections.formula:
sₚ² = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²] / (n₁+n₂−2)
SE = √[sₚ²(1/n₁+1/n₂)]
t = [(x̄₁−x̄₂)−D₀] / SE
df = n₁+n₂−2
sections.trap: sₚ² is a VARIANCE. If the problem gives SDs 2 and 3, square them to 4 and 9. Do not average SDs or forget the n−1 weights.
sections.source: Two Sample Means, slides 10–16

sections.title: Unknown and unequal variances: Welch
sections.body: Welch uses each sample’s own variance in the SE rather than a pooled variance. Its adjusted df account for unequal variances and sample sizes; they are generally not n₁+n₂−2 and can be noninteger. Know which formula belongs to which assumption.
sections.formula:
SE_W = √(s₁²/n₁+s₂²/n₂)
t_W = [(x̄₁−x̄₂)−D₀]/SE_W
df_W = (s₁²/n₁+s₂²/n₂)² / [(s₁²/n₁)²/(n₁−1)+(s₂²/n₂)²/(n₂−1)]
sections.example: For n₁=10, n₂=12, s₁=2, s₂=3, Welch SE≈1.0724 and adjusted df≈19.19. This differs from pooled SE≈1.1124 and df=20.
sections.trap: Using the unpooled SE together with pooled df mixes two methods. Read whether equal variances are actually assumed.
sections.source: Two Sample Means, slides 9, 21–22

sections.title: Tails, critical values, and Excel
sections.body: Hₐ determines the direction of the difference: >0, <0, or ≠0. For a two-sided test, compare |t| with the supplied positive t critical value or use a two-sided p-value. T.TEST works on raw data arrays: tails=1 or 2; type=2 for independent equal-variance t and type=3 for Welch. Type=1 is paired data, not this deck’s independent design.
sections.formula:
Pooled two-sided critical value: =T.INV.2T(alpha,n₁+n₂−2)
Two-sided p-value from statistic: =T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df)
Raw data: =T.TEST(array1,array2,2,2) [pooled]
Raw data: =T.TEST(array1,array2,2,3) [Welch]
sections.example: At t≈2.697, df=20, and supplied two-sided 5% cutoff 2.086, reject equality. A matching pooled 95% difference CI is 3±2.086(1.1124)≈(.679,5.321).
sections.trap: The slides contain inconsistent labels/arithmetic in their worked example. Use the clearly stated SD-versus-variance definitions and correct formulas here. T.TEST syntax is an added Excel-recognition aid.
sections.source: Two Sample Means, slides 17–20; formula-recognition extension for T.TEST

topics.title: Chi-square: categories & expected counts
topics.summary: Work with category counts, calculate what H₀ predicts, and sum squared discrepancies. Distinguish one categorical variable from two.

sections.title: Which chi-square test?
sections.body: Goodness of fit asks whether ONE categorical variable follows specified category proportions, such as equal brand preference or a fair die. Independence asks whether TWO categorical variables are associated in an r×c contingency table. For independence, H₀ says independent; Hₐ says associated/dependent.
sections.formula:
Goodness of fit H₀: category proportions match the specified distribution
Independence H₀: the two categorical variables are independent
sections.example: Favorite brand alone across five brands → goodness of fit. Gender and favorite brand in a 2×3 table → independence.
sections.trap: Two categorical variables are not two sample MEANS. A statistically significant association does not by itself establish causation.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 3–6; Practice Exam, Q23–24, Q30

sections.title: Expected counts under H₀
sections.body: Expected counts describe what the null predicts, not what you observed. For goodness of fit, multiply n by each hypothesized probability. For independence, expected cell count comes from its row and column totals; row and column proportions combine under independence. Use counts, not percentages, in the chi-square statistic.
sections.formula:
Goodness of fit: Eᵢ=n×pᵢ₀
Independence: Eᵢⱼ=(row totalᵢ×column totalⱼ)/grand total
sections.example: A fair die rolled 180 times has expected count 30 per face. A table cell with row total 120, column total 80, grand total 400 has E=120×80/400=24.
sections.trap: Expected does not mean an equal split unless H₀ actually specifies equal probabilities. Keep expected decimals until the final result.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 8–9, 12–14, 17; Practice Exam, Q25, Q27

sections.title: The chi-square statistic and right-tail logic
sections.body: Each contribution measures squared observed-minus-expected discrepancy relative to the expected count. Sum across ALL categories/cells. Large discrepancies produce a large χ² and evidence against H₀. Contributions are nonnegative, so the rejection region is always in the right tail.
sections.formula:
χ² = Σ[(O−E)²/E]
Reject for χ² > supplied right-tail critical value
sections.example: If two categories have observed counts 60 and 40 with expected counts 50 and 50, χ²=(10²/50)+(−10)²/50=4. With df=1 and 5% cutoff 3.841, reject.
sections.trap: Square O−E, then divide by E. Do not divide by O. An association alternative can be “two-sided” in ordinary language, but χ² itself still uses a right-tail probability.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 8–11; Practice Exam, Q28

sections.title: Degrees of freedom and expected-count checks
sections.body: For an r×c independence table, df=(r−1)(c−1). For a goodness-of-fit test with k categories and fully specified probabilities, df=k−1. The course requires all EXPECTED counts to be at least 5. Observations should be independent and categories mutually exclusive; normality of individual observations is not required.
sections.formula:
Independence df=(r−1)(c−1)
Goodness of fit df=k−1 [no parameters estimated]
Course check: every E ≥ 5
sections.example: A 3×4 table has df=(3−1)(4−1)=6. Five equally preferred brands have df=4, not 5. Count table rows/columns without the totals row or column.
sections.trap: The requirement is about expected counts, not every observed count. Totals are not extra categories.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 10, 18; Practice Exam, Q24, Q26, Q29

sections.title: Excel and writing the conclusion
sections.body: CHISQ.DIST.RT gives the p-value from an observed statistic and df. CHISQ.INV.RT gives a right-tail critical value from α and df. CHISQ.TEST uses observed and expected count ranges directly and returns a p-value. Compare that p-value to α and describe the specific category distribution or association.
sections.formula:
p-value: =CHISQ.DIST.RT(statistic,df)
Critical value: =CHISQ.INV.RT(alpha,df)
Counts in ranges: =CHISQ.TEST(observed_range,expected_range)
sections.example: Five-category goodness of fit at 5% uses =CHISQ.INV.RT(0.05,4). If a 3×4 independence test rejects, say there is evidence the two categorical variables are associated.
sections.trap: INV finds a cutoff from a probability; DIST finds a probability from a statistic. Failure to reject independence does not prove independence.
sections.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 18–20; Practice Exam, Q24; CHISQ syntax is an Excel-recognition aid

flashcards.front: What is a sampling distribution?
flashcards.back: The distribution of a statistic over repeated random samples of the same size. For x̄, its mean is μ and its SE is σ/√n.

flashcards.front: SD versus SE: what does each measure?
flashcards.back: SD measures spread of individual observations; SE measures spread of a statistic across samples. Estimated SE of x̄ is s/√n.

flashcards.front: How much must n increase to halve SE?
flashcards.back: Multiply n by 4, since SE is proportional to 1/√n.

flashcards.front: Does the CLT make the original population normal?
flashcards.back: No. It makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal for sufficiently large n. The course uses about 30 as a rule of thumb.

flashcards.front: In Excel, what gives P(x̄>a) when σ is known?
flashcards.back: =1-NORM.DIST(a,mu,sigma/SQRT(n),TRUE). The spread is SE, and 1− makes it a right tail.

flashcards.front: What does 95% confidence mean?
flashcards.back: About 95% of intervals made by this method across repeated samples cover the fixed population parameter. It is not 95% of individual observations.
flashcards.source: CI Proportions, slides 3–4; Practice Exam, Q8

flashcards.front: When do you use z versus t for a mean CI?
flashcards.back: Known population σ → x̄±z*σ/√n. Unknown σ → x̄±t*s/√n with df=n−1.
flashcards.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 6–10

flashcards.front: What are the common two-sided z* values?
flashcards.back: 90%: 1.645; 95%: 1.960; 99%: 2.576. Higher confidence means a wider interval.
flashcards.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slide 7

flashcards.front: How do you find the t* for a 90% CI with n=20 in Excel?
flashcards.back: =T.INV.2T(0.10,19). Input alpha=.10 and df=n−1=19.
flashcards.source: Practice Exam, Q14; CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slide 10

flashcards.front: A CI is (14,22). What are the point estimate and margin of error?
flashcards.back: Point estimate=(14+22)/2=18. Margin of error=(22−14)/2=4.
flashcards.source: CI Sigma Known and Unknown, slides 5–7

flashcards.front: What SE belongs in a one-proportion confidence interval?
flashcards.back: √[p̂(1−p̂)/n], using the SAMPLE proportion p̂=x/n.

flashcards.front: What SE belongs in a one-proportion test of p=p₀?
flashcards.back: √[p₀(1−p₀)/n], using the NULL proportion. Then z=(p̂−p₀)/SE₀.

flashcards.front: When do you pool two sample proportions?
flashcards.back: For the usual test of equal population proportions: p̂_pool=(x₁+x₂)/(n₁+n₂). Do not pool for an ordinary CI for p₁−p₂.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 24–28

flashcards.front: What is the SE for a CI for p₁−p₂?
flashcards.back: √[p̂₁(1−p̂₁)/n₁+p̂₂(1−p̂₂)/n₂]. Each group keeps its own estimated proportion.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, handwritten slides 27–28

flashcards.front: If two separate proportion CIs overlap, are the populations necessarily equal?
flashcards.back: No. Use a CI or test for their difference. Nonoverlap supports a difference; overlap does not prove equality.

flashcards.front: What chooses the tail of a hypothesis test?
flashcards.back: The alternative hypothesis: > means right tail; < means left tail; ≠ means two tails. Equality stays in H₀.

flashcards.front: What is a p-value, and when do you reject?
flashcards.back: Assuming H₀, the probability of evidence at least as extreme in the direction(s) of Hₐ. Reject if p≤α; otherwise fail to reject.

flashcards.front: Type I versus Type II error?
flashcards.back: Type I: reject a true H₀ (false alarm; rate α). Type II: fail to reject a false H₀ (miss; rate β). Power=1−β.

flashcards.front: How do you calculate a two-sided z p-value from a negative z?
flashcards.back: Use 2[1−Φ(|z|)], or Excel =2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(z),TRUE)). Take the absolute value first.
flashcards.source: Hypothesis Testing, slides 30–31; Practice Exam, Q22

flashcards.front: If α is fixed, what does increasing n usually do to power?
flashcards.back: It increases power and reduces β for a fixed nonzero effect. The nominal Type I error rate remains α.

flashcards.front: What decides pooled t versus Welch t?
flashcards.back: Unknown population variances assumed equal → pooled t. Unknown and unequal/not assumed equal → Welch t. Equal sample sizes alone do not justify pooling.

flashcards.front: What is the pooled sample variance?
flashcards.back: sₚ²=[(n₁−1)s₁²+(n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁+n₂−2). It weights sample VARIANCES by their df.

flashcards.front: What SE and df go with pooled two-sample t?
flashcards.back: SE=√[sₚ²(1/n₁+1/n₂)] and df=n₁+n₂−2.

flashcards.front: What SE goes with Welch t?
flashcards.back: √(s₁²/n₁+s₂²/n₂), together with Welch adjusted df—not automatically n₁+n₂−2.

flashcards.front: Independent groups or paired data: same people before and after?
flashcards.back: Paired. Analyze within-person differences rather than treating the two measurements as independent groups. This is a design-recognition extension.
flashcards.source: Two Sample Means, slide 4 (independence assumption); recognition extension

flashcards.front: Goodness of fit versus independence?
flashcards.back: Goodness of fit: one categorical variable versus specified proportions. Independence: association between two categorical variables in a contingency table.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slide 3; Practice Exam, Q23, Q30

flashcards.front: What are the expected counts?
flashcards.back: Goodness of fit: E=n×null probability. Independence: E=(row total×column total)/grand total.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 8–9, 12–14; Practice Exam, Q25, Q27

flashcards.front: What are the chi-square statistic and its rejection tail?
flashcards.back: χ²=Σ(O−E)²/E. All contributions are nonnegative; the rejection region is always in the RIGHT tail.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 8–11

flashcards.front: What are the df formulas and course count condition?
flashcards.back: Independence df=(r−1)(c−1). Goodness of fit df=k−1 when probabilities are fully specified. The course requires every EXPECTED count≥5.
flashcards.source: Chi Square Test of Independence, slides 10, 18; Practice Exam, Q24, Q29

flashcards.front: CHISQ.DIST.RT versus CHISQ.INV.RT?
flashcards.back: DIST.RT(statistic,df) returns the right-tail p-value. INV.RT(alpha,df) returns the right-tail critical value.
flashcards.source: Practice Exam, Q24; Chi Square Test of Independence, slide 19

plan.title: Diagnose before studying
plan.description: Do a mixed diagnostic without notes. For every answer, name the method and the reason; mark guesses even if correct. Use the topic scores to choose what to revisit.

plan.title: Learn the decision map
plan.description: Read the six short topic lessons. Practice classifying variable type, one versus two samples, mean versus proportion, known versus unknown σ, and alternative direction before touching a calculator.

plan.title: Work the algebra by hand
plan.description: Calculate one z interval, one t interval, one proportion interval, one pooled two-mean t, one pooled two-proportion z, and one chi-square expected-count calculation. Write SE as a separate step each time.

plan.title: Retrieve, then repair
plan.description: Answer flashcards before revealing the backs. Drill missed topics and explain why each distractor is wrong. Redo misses later without looking at the explanation.

plan.title: Rehearse the real format
plan.description: Take a fresh 20-question mixed mock with a 70-minute timer, as described in the practice PDF. Use a calculator and only the reference values supplied with the mock. That averages 3.5 minutes per question; move past a stuck calculation and return.

plan.title: Make the last review count
plan.description: Review misses and guesses by cause: method, SE, tail, df, algebra, or interpretation. Rewrite the right rule from memory, then solve a different question on that rule. Aim for repeated success on fresh questions, not memorized letters.
